entry.title: Development :: RE: Long lost cheat codes
entry.dc:creator: elizacommunities
entry.dc:subject: Development
entry.content:
Author: elizacommunities
Posted: Wed Nov 18, 2026 7:20 am (GMT 0)

Thanks for sharing these — the Taz-Mania one is a lovely find. A proper cheat menu hidden behind a pause-and-button sequence is exactly the sort of thing that would have been passed around by word of mouth back in the day, and having the exact steps written down makes it genuinely usable rather than just a curiosity.

The Chicago Syndicate details stood out for me too. Explaining not just the code itself but where to enter it — Training mode, Hyde Park, holding the buttons for 256 frames — and then the Valentine's Day condition for invincibility, really shows how much careful checking went into this. That context is what turns a code list into something people can actually try.

I would be keen to see Strider 2 or Chakan next, if either of those is on your list. Thanks again for taking the time to document all of this so clearly.

entry.title: Development :: RE: [AI] Someone ran my homebrew through an LLM
entry.dc:creator: ArugulaZ
entry.dc:subject: Development
entry.content:
Author: ArugulaZ
Subject: And this was the toned down version of this post!
Posted: Wed Nov 18, 2026 12:03 am (GMT 0)

Clearly, Segarule doesn't.

There's a difference between using artwork from a forty year old game, from an artist who was already paid for their work, and parasitizing recent code from starving artists who either are doing it out of enthusiasm or for the slim hope of payment.

The person who made the Master System version of Bruce Lee made no claims that the original artwork was theirs. It's a well known, and very old, game. It can safely be deduced from this information that the artwork is not theirs. Using that as an excuse to lift recent code from others without their consent is frankly kind of craven and pathetic.

"Well, I can steal any code I want from you, because YOU made a Pac-Man clone!" Yeah, him and just about everyone else on the planet. Why does taking inspiration from a forty year old source give you carte blanche to steal whatever you want from hard-working coders? Try applying that same attitude to a Disney movie, typically inspired by literature in the public domain, and see where it gets you. The only difference is that they have well-paid lawyers, and the average basement coder can't even afford to live above ground.

Personally, I try to keep my software as original as possible. Even the artwork is built from scratch, because I want them to be MY games, not someone else's work. And they will remain my games. I'll put this as clearly as possible so there's no misunderstanding: you are prohibited from using JessCREATIONS games, code, and audiovisuals to create derivative works with AI, or to train a large language model.

If you use my code to teach yourself coding, or study the artwork to teach yourself how to make sprites and tiles, I have no issue with that. I'm happy to offer that as a resource to other humans, as 8-bit game design is a fading art; one I'd like to keep alive for as long as possible. But if you're just going to chuck all my work into the Regurgitron and have a computer poop out something in fifteen minutes, no, you don't get to do that. What makes you think anyone would be okay with that?

It's bad enough that AI is taking peoples' work without their permission. It's worse that AI is turning internet users into shameless, entitled parasites. It's 2026, for God's sake! BASIC and object-oriented programming has made the game design process easier than it's ever been, and you still want a shortcut? How spoon-fed do you want this process to be?

Quote
A similar thing happened to me recently, when someone grabbed the ROM of my Bruce Lee remake, and ran it through Claude to have it slop-ported to Amiga and Atari ST. Last I checked, he was still asking for donations for all of "his" hard work on itch.io.
When I called him out for it, he finally bothered to contact me, and we made some small amends, but even after that, when he already knew well how I feel about it, he kept messing with my stuff, producing "enhanced" AGA and STE versions with horribly mangled variations of my artwork.

The thing is that when we talked, he genuinely didn't give the impression of having ill intentions, and I absolutely believe him. There just seem to be people who can't imagine why someone wouldn't be okay with having his stuff fed to an LLM. It's freely available on the internet, and that's all the justification needed, apparently.
The guy who did this to your work probably thinks he's doing you a favor.

I really don't know where this will all end. The mutual respect between developers isn't something that applies to people always on the lookout for new stuff to feed to their LLM of choice, it seems, and the consequences are that a lot of communitues just find out that they have never been communities to begin with, rather two groups of people with little overlap, who just happened to gather around the same camp fire.

Personally, I hope Ed Zitron is right and the unsustainable financing of the AI bubble makes it crash rather sooner than later, removing the models from the hands of non-professional users. I just hope that the amount of digital asbestos that gets produced up to that point will not have killed what used to be the comfy niches of the internet entirely.

Let’s reserve judgment on the game until we can play it. There’s a range of opinions here and the only wrong attitude is to say someone else’s is wrong. LLMs are a tool, but that doesn’t make using them or not using them a superior position. But for the foreseeable future, we are segregating homebrew/ports where any content was generated by an LLM from those without, to help people easily filter on that axis.
